WITH x AS (SELECT b.bill_id, sum(l.qty*l.unit_cost-p.qty*p.unit_cost) diff
FROM finance_vendor_bill_lines l JOIN finance_vendor_bills b USING(bill_id)
JOIN erp_purchase_order_lines p ON p.po_id=b.po_id AND p.sku=l.sku
JOIN finance_vendor_payments vp ON vp.bill_id=b.bill_id AND abs(vp.amount-b.amount)<0.01
WHERE l.qty*l.unit_cost-p.qty*p.unit_cost>0.005 GROUP BY 1),
t AS (SELECT bill_id, string_agg(DISTINCT kind, '+') kinds, max(caught) c, sum(amount_over) ao FROM truth.truth.bill_issues GROUP BY 1)
SELECT t.kinds, t.c, count(*) n, round(sum(x.diff),2) analyst_excess, round(sum(t.ao),2) truth_over
FROM x LEFT JOIN t USING(bill_id) GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 3 DESC

content.text:
I graded F2 as **full** against P4 (supplier bills that don't match the PO and the receipt) and saved `grade.json`.

- **The flagged bills are all real.** Every one of the 13,949 paid-in-full bills the analyst flags is a planted P4 issue that accounts payable didn't catch (t372).
  - The 3,390 bills billing more quantity than was received total $2,087,672.59, exactly the truth figure.
  - The 9,501 bills priced above the PO total $759,383.05; truth has $759,382.90.
  - The rest are bills with more than one planted problem.
- **The catch rate matches.** The analyst says accounts payable short-paid about 30% of overbilled bills. Truth agrees: for example, 1,713 of 5,542 quantity problems were caught (t371).
- **The finding identifies the mechanism with evidence from the records.** That's why I gave it full credit rather than partly, even though its size falls well short (below).

The grade notes what the finding gets wrong:

- **It undersizes the problem.** It puts the loss at $317K a year; the key says $876.6K.
  - The analyst's total counts only the quantity and price problems.
  - The truth also has $2.75M in uncaught duplicate bills and $2.45M in freight not on the PO (t371).
  - Duplicates (about $2.73M) appear only as a next step, and freight only as amounts accounts payable withheld.
- **It hedges where it shouldn't.** It says special-order quantities and higher unit costs might have been owed. Truth marks all of them as overbilling.

If you read "partly" more strictly, as covering only part of a multi-part problem, this could be argued down to partly, since only two of the four overbilling types are in its total.
